2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern: The stratified random household survey achieved a 95.2% participation rate among eligible housing units (396/416), and item-level missingness was low (0% to 6.6% for most variables; 12.4% for income) and rigorously handled using multiple imputation with fully conditional specification across 10 imputed datasets incorporating auxiliary variables.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Moderate concern: Multiple linear and logistic regressions controlled for respondent gender, education, marital status, age, ethnicity, household size, homeownership, and concurrent financial, physical, and social resources, while accounting for compound clustering and finite population correction. However, the cross-sectional design precludes temporal precedence (reverse causality/simultaneity between water expenditures, storage investments, and consumption), and spatial/institutional confounders such as terrain elevation/water pressure, distance to BWD mains, and formal legal land title versus informal settlement status were not directly measured.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / weak-to-adequate concern: Institutional access to the federally authorized municipal utility (Baguio Water District, BWD) was operationalized via self-reported connection tiers (none, shared/some other way, own household metered connection) alongside self-reported homeownership and permanent/boarding tenancy stratification, and qualitatively contextualized with connection fee rules (₱6,000 fee plus ₱4,000–₱8,000 piping costs, case-by-case installment plans, and informal 'under the table' processing barriers). However, formal legal land tenure, municipal eligibility ordinances, and official BWD billing/meter records were not independently verified.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High / some concern: All exposures and outcomes relied on respondent self-report and recall during a single dry season that was wetter than usual. Notably, the author documents systematic misclassification in the hypothetical social borrowing network exposure (water-secure households that had never needed to borrow reported zero network size), recall bias in estimated dry-season water consumption, and reliance on unvalidated subjective 11-point scales for cleanliness and ease without objective water-quality or meter verification.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-weak concern: Water security was operationalized across four distinct dimensions—reported consumption (liters per capita per day), perceived cleanliness (PCA score of five 11-point items for non-drinking domestic uses), perceived ease (11-point scale dichotomized at 8–10), and affordability (monthly water expenses as percentage of income dichotomized at <=10%)—with enumerator assistance to estimate container volumes. However, measures were unvalidated, relied on recall during an atypically wet dry season, excluded drinking-water safety from the cleanliness scale, and lacked physical or microbiological verification.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell on pre-registration: No pre-registered study protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported, and two outcomes (perceived ease and affordability) as well as social network exposures were categorized/dichotomized post hoc based on observed data distributions and skewness. Mitigating this concern, the author reports that robustness checks using alternate functional forms of dependent variables and covariate subsets produced consistent results, and null or unexpected regression findings (for savings, homeownership, and borrowing networks) are transparently reported.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: Within the study neighborhood (Pinget), selection bias for the quantitative component was very low, using an updated neighborhood census sampling frame (1,793 housing units), stratified random sampling by subdistrict (purok) and tenancy status, and a 95.2% response rate (N = 396). However, Pinget was purposively selected as a single neighborhood within Baguio City, and the qualitative interview subsample (n = 18) was purposively sampled from survey respondents with intentional oversampling of women (15 women, 3 men), limiting external generalizability beyond Pinget.

domain_ratings.justification: The paper states two explicit study aims: (a) examining how specific financial, physical, and social household resources are associated with four water security measures (reported consumption, perceived cleanliness, perceived ease, and affordability), and (b) examining how households acquire and use financial, physical, and social resources to improve water security.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Collected data comprise a stratified random household survey (N = 396) measuring household resources, sociodemographic controls, and four water security indicators to address Aim 1, paired with 18 purposively sampled in-depth interviews with household water managers exploring resource acquisition and use to address Aim 2.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: An interpretive/descriptive qualitative interview approach is well suited to Aim 2, uncovering household decision-making, saving strategies, utility application barriers, and neighbor water-sharing norms that cannot be captured by structured survey items alone.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Eighteen in-person, audiotaped semi-structured interviews (~50 minutes each) were conducted with purposively sampled household water managers across varied water sources, water security levels, and demographics, using an advance topic guide and multilingual research assistant translation in the participant's preferred language.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 10 (p. 497, In-Depth Interviews - Sampling and implementation)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: All transcripts were systematically reviewed and analyzed using qualitative memoing, first-level descriptive coding in NVivo 9, and second-stage focused/analytic coding to develop emergent themes across resource domains.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: Qualitative interpretations across financial, physical, and social resource themes are grounded in direct verbatim participant quotations and concrete local cost figures (e.g., drum/tank prices and BWD connection/installment fees), although coding was performed by a single researcher without reported intercoder checks or member checking.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: There is clear methodological alignment linking Aim 2, purposive subsample selection from surveyed water managers, semi-structured interview topics, two-cycle thematic coding, and narrative interpretation organized by financial, physical, and social resources.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the participants representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: For the target study community of Pinget, the research team canvassed the neighborhood to update a census list to 1,793 housing units, stratified by purok (subdistrict) and tenancy status (permanent or boarding), randomly selected 25% per stratum, and achieved a 95.2% participation rate among 416 eligible units (N = 396). The author transparently notes that findings generalize to Pinget rather than all of Baguio City.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 7, 20 (pp. 494, 507, Household Surveys & Study Strengths and Limitations)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are measurements appropriate regarding both the outcome and intervention (or exposure)?
domain_ratings.justification: Both exposures and outcomes relied entirely on self-report and recall without objective meter or water-quality verification, and the paper explicitly documents systematic misclassification in the social borrowing network exposure (water-secure households who never needed to borrow answered zero to hypothetical borrowing questions), recall underestimation risks in consumption, unvalidated water security scales, omission of drinking water from the cleanliness PCA, and data-driven dichotomization of ease and affordability.

Survey unit response was 95.2% (396/416), item missingness was at most 6.6% on all outcome and non-income variables (12.4% for income), and missing values were rigorously addressed via multiple imputation with fully conditional specification across 10 imputed datasets with auxiliary variables.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 7, 9 (pp. 494, 496, Missing data and multiple imputation)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the confounders accounted for in the design and analysis?
domain_ratings.justification: Stratified sampling and multivariable linear/logistic regressions adjusted simultaneously for financial, physical, and social resources alongside respondent gender, education, marital status, age, ethnicity, and household size, with clustering adjustment for shared compounds; however, residual confounding from unmeasured topographic elevation, formal land title, and cross-sectional simultaneity remains possible.

domain_ratings.domain_name: During the study period, is the intervention administered (or exposure occurred) as intended?
domain_ratings.justification: In this cross-sectional observational study of dry-season household resources and water security, data collection occurred during a single dry season that was wetter than usual due to chance weather variation, making it uncertain whether typical dry-season scarcity and resource-use conditions operated as intended during respondents' recall window.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 20 (p. 507, Study Strengths and Limitations)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: The author provides a clear rationale for combining quantitative regression modeling (to test population-level resource-outcome associations in Pinget) with qualitative interviews (to explain how households acquire, save for, and mobilize resources to navigate water insecurity).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Integration was achieved at the sampling level (nesting the 18 purposive interviewees within the 396 surveyed household water managers), data collection level (field observations informing the interview guide), and interpretation level (structuring quantitative and qualitative findings around identical financial, physical, and social resource constructs).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the outputs of the integration adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: Combined interpretation demonstrates not only that income, tank/drum capacity, and household BWD connections predict better water security, but also how financial constraints (₱10,000–₱14,000 total BWD connection costs and restrictive installment plans) mediate access to those physical assets and shape policy recommendations.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 15-22 (pp. 502-509, Results and Discussion & Conclusions)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: Divergences between regression results and interview accounts are explicitly examined—specifically why savings had minimal direct regression associations (likely mediated by prior purchases of tanks, drums, and BWD meters) and why borrowing networks showed null or negative associations with perceived ease (due to hypothetical survey item misinterpretation by water-secure households and social discomfort around borrowing).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 15-19 (pp. 502-506, Discussion of key associations & Qualitative Findings)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: While sampling, response rate, missing-data imputation, and mixed-methods integration are strong, the quantitative component suffers from unvalidated self-report/recall outcomes, documented differential misclassification in the hypothetical social-resource exposure (criterion 3.2 rated No), and cross-sectional data collection during an unusually wet dry season, while the qualitative component omits researcher reflexivity regarding translator-mediated interviews and intercoder checks.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Mason (2014) is a primary mixed-methods study investigating household financial, physical, and social resources and water security in Pinget, an urban barangay of Baguio City, Philippines, combining a stratified random household survey (N = 396; 95.2% response rate) with nested purposive in-depth interviews (n = 18). Appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT 2018, using Qualitative 1.1–1.5, Quantitative non-randomized/analytical cross-sectional 3.1–3.5, and Mixed Methods 5.1–5.5), the study exhibits notable strengths in probability sampling within the target neighborhood, low missing data rigorously handled via multiple imputation, multivariable adjustment with compound-level clustering, and transparent mixed-methods integration—particularly in explaining divergences between null/counterintuitive survey coefficients and rich qualitative accounts of savings and neighbor water-sharing. Methodological concerns center on the quantitative component's cross-sectional observational design (precluding causal/temporal inference between household investments, water expenditures, and outcomes), field collection during an unusually wet dry season, reliance on unvalidated self-report and recall measures of water consumption and perceived cleanliness/ease without physical or microbiological verification, post-hoc dichotomization of two outcomes, and documented systematic misclassification in the hypothetical social borrowing network exposure. Per MMAT 2018 rules, no composite numeric score is calculated; overall methodological concern is judged as Moderate.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (14 Yes, 2 No [3.2, 5.5], 1 Can't tell [3.5]; no numeric score per MMAT 2018 guidance, with overall quality bounded by self-report/exposure misclassification and cross-sectional limitations in the quantitative component)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Primary mixed-methods study combining an analytical cross-sectional stratified random household survey (N = 396) analyzed via linear and logistic multiple regression with purposively sampled semi-structured in-depth interviews (n = 18)

raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The Methods section explicitly specifies and executes a primary mixed-methods empirical design pairing a quantitative household survey (N = 396) for Aim 1 with qualitative in-depth interviews (n = 18) for Aim 2, integrating both strands across financial, physical, and social resource domains. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, MMAT is the single matching appraisal instrument, applying Qualitative items 1.1–1.5, Quantitative non-randomized items 3.1–3.5 (matching the analytical cross-sectional multivariable regression component), and Mixed-Methods integration items 5.1–5.5.
